entities.summary:
The Temple of Fides (Latin: Aedes Fidei) on the Capitoline Hill in Rome, one of Rome's most ancient and revered temples, was dedicated to Fides (Latin: 'Faith', 'Trust', 'Good Faith') — the Roman divine personification of trust, reliability, and the sacred obligation to keep one's word, a virtue considered foundational to Rome's social and political fabric and particularly essential to treaty relationships, oaths, and the bonds between citizens.

Fides was among the most ancient Roman deities, with Livy attributing the original Temple of Fides to King Numa Pompilius (Rome's legendary second king, traditionally reigning 715-673 BCE). The temple on the Capitoline was rebuilt by the censor Aulus Atilius Calatinus in 254 BCE and subsequently restored multiple times. Its Capitoline location — alongside the Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus and the Temple of Juno Moneta — placed Fides among Rome's most sacred divine figures.

The priestly cult of Fides required the three chief priests (flamines maiores) to sacrifice to her with their right hands wrapped in white cloth — symbolizing that the right hand of oath and good faith should remain protected and pure. The Dextrarum iunctio (joining of right hands) as a symbol of marriage, agreement, and mutual faith in Roman culture reflected Fides's centrality to Roman social bonds. The temple's Capitoline location associated Fides with the divine validation of Rome's most sacred oaths — the swearing of treaties before Jupiter on the Capitoline required Fides as divine witness. The temple embodies Rome's institutionalization of abstract civic virtues as divine beings requiring cult and worship.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Temple of Fides — representing Rome's institutionalization of good faith as a divine obligation, housing the divine witness to Rome's most sacred treaty oaths on the Capitoline, and exemplifying the Roman practice of deifying abstract civic virtues — is an important window into Rome's distinctive religious-civic integration.
